title: Returning a structure from a function

visuals.title: Match each idea to its meaning

pairs.meaning: A function whose return type is a structure
Sends the whole structure back; a copy lands in the caller's variable
The returned structure is stored in the variable s
One function giving back several related values (total, average, grade)
The other way to hand back values: write into a reference parameter
Dangerous: the local variable is destroyed when the function ends

stages.name: 1. Build
stages.detail: Inside the function we make a local structure r and fill its members.

stages.name: 2. return r;
stages.detail: The function ends and a COPY of r is sent back.

stages.name: 3. Cleanup
stages.detail: The function's own variables (including r) are destroyed.

stages.name: 4. Store
stages.detail: The caller stores the copy: Point s = add(p, q); now s holds the values.

goal: After this you can write a function that returns a structure (Student read(), Point add(Point a, Point b)), use it to return several values together, and explain why you must never return a pointer to a local variable.
warmup: At the university fee counter you give your roll number and the clerk gives you ONE slip with your name, total fee and due date printed together. You did not need three separate pieces of paper. A function that returns a structure is that slip: one object carrying several related answers.
definition: A function can have a structure as its return type, for example Point add(Point a, Point b). The function builds a structure (often a local variable r), and return r; sends the whole structure back. The caller receives a copy and usually stores it in its own variable: Point s = add(p, q);. This is a clean way to return several values at once, because a normal return can give back only one value but a structure can hold many members.
howItWorks: Look at the first trace and the call stack. add has its own boxes a, b and r. When return r; runs, the three boxes are about to be destroyed, so C++ copies the values of r into the place where the result is needed: the variable s in main. That is why returning a structure BY VALUE is safe: s has its own copy. The second trace shows the pattern for several answers: evaluate calculates total, average and grade, puts them in a Result and returns it. In main, res.total, res.average and res.grade give the three answers. There is another way to give back values: pass a reference parameter and fill it, like void evaluate(int m1, int m2, int m3, Result &r). Returning is usually easier to read, because the call evaluate(80, 75, 90) can be used like a value. Filling a reference avoids the copy, which matters only for very large structures. Danger zone: never return a pointer or reference to a local variable (for example return &s; where s is a local structure). The local variable is destroyed when the function ends, so the pointer points to a dead box. g++ warns 'address of local variable returned', and using it gives garbage or a crash. Return the structure by value instead.

worked.problem: Write a function add that takes two Point structures and returns a new Point whose x and y are the sums.

STORE the returned Point in s

sample.title: Point add(Point a, Point b)

explanation.text: A structure with two ints.
The return type is Point, a structure. The parameters are structures passed by value.
Build the answer in a local structure.
Fill each member.
Returns the whole structure at once: both x and y travel back together.
The returned structure is copied into s. add(p, q) can be used wherever a Point is needed.
Print with the dot: s.x and s.y.

steps.note: The program starts at main().
main creates two Point variables p and q.
The call add(p, q) passes COPIES of p and q into the parameters a and b. The result of the call will be a Point that is stored into s.
Inside add we build a new local structure r. It is empty for now.
r.y = 3 + 1 = 4. The new Point is complete.
The whole structure r is returned: a COPY of r travels back to main. Then add ends and a, b and r are destroyed.
The returned copy is stored in s. s is now (6, 4). The local r is gone, but s has its own copy of the values.
main prints the members of s.
The program ends.

worked.problem: A function must give back the total, the average and the grade of three subjects. Show how a structure lets one function return all three, and trace the exact output.
pseudocode: grade: 81.6667 is not >= 85 but is >= 70, so B
STORE in res and PRINT its members

sample.title: Returning several values in one structure

explanation.text: One structure holds three related answers.
The function gives back a Result: three answers from one function.
The total of the three marks.
3.0 forces a decimal result.
The grade ladder: A, B, C, else F.
Return the whole structure.
Store the returned structure in a variable.
Use res.total, res.average and res.grade.

steps.note: The program starts at main().
main calls evaluate(80, 75, 90). The three marks are copied into m1, m2, m3.
evaluate builds a local Result r with three members: total, average, grade.
245 / 3.0 = 81.6667 (3.0 makes the division a decimal division).
81.6667 >= 85 is false, so we go to the next test.
81.6667 >= 70 is true, so grade is B.
The whole structure (three values) is returned in one go. A copy goes back to main and evaluate's variables are destroyed.
The returned copy is stored in res. Now main has all three results together.
main prints the three members of res.
The program ends.

variations.way: Return a structure by value: Point add(Point a, Point b)
variations.when: The normal choice. The function builds a result and gives it back.

variations.way: Function that reads and returns: Student readStudent()
variations.when: You want a function that creates a filled record from keyboard input.

variations.way: Return a structure with several results
variations.when: You need total, average and grade together.
variations.example:
Result res = evaluate(80, 75, 90);
cout << res.total << res.grade;

variations.way: Fill a reference parameter: void evaluate(int m1, int m2, int m3, Result &r)
variations.when: You want to avoid copying a big structure, or the function already returns something else.

variations.way: Return a pointer to a local (do NOT do this)
variations.when: Never: the local variable dies when the function ends.
variations.example: Student* make() { Student s = {"A", 1}; return &s; }  // wrong

variations.when: You need only one member right now.

mistakes.error: error: could not convert '(a.Point::x + b.Point::x)' from 'int' to 'Point'
error: cannot convert 'Point' to 'int' in initialization

mistakes.right:
Point s = add(p, q);
cout << s.x << " " << s.y;
mistakes.error: error: no match for 'operator<<' (operand types are 'std::ostream' {aka 'std::basic_ostream<char>'} and 'Point')
warning: address of local variable 's' returned (only a warning, but the pointer points to a destroyed variable: using it gives garbage or a crash)
The compiler may only warn about a missing return. The function then returns garbage, so the answer is wrong. Always end with return r;.

examTips: When a function must give back several related values, return a structure (or fill reference parameters). Mention both ways and say which one you used.
The return type is the structure name: Result evaluate(...), not void and not int.
Store the returned structure in a variable of the same type: Result res = evaluate(...). You cannot cout a whole structure; print its members.
In a trace, show the local r being copied into the caller's variable before the function's boxes disappear.
Never return a pointer or reference to a local variable. Say why: the variable is destroyed when the function ends.
romanSummary: Function poora structure return kar sakta hai: Point add(Point a, Point b). Return type mein structure ka naam likhte hain.
Function ke andar local structure r bana kar members fill karte hain aur return r; likhte hain.
Caller ko copy milti hai: Point s = add(p, q); is liye ek saath kai related values (total, average, grade) wapas aa jati hain.
Dusra tareeqa reference parameter hai: void evaluate(..., Result &r), jis mein function jawab bhar deta hai.
Local variable ka pointer kabhi return na karein, kyun ke function khatam hote hi wo variable destroy ho jata hai.

quiz.prompt: Why return a structure from a function?
options: To give back several related values together
Because return cannot give a number
To make the program faster always
quiz.answer: To give back several related values together
quiz.explanation: A structure holds many members, so one return can carry several results.

quiz.prompt: How do you store the result of Result evaluate(int, int, int)?
quiz.explanation: The variable must be of the structure type that the function returns.

quiz.prompt: What does the caller receive when the function runs return r; with a local structure r?
quiz.explanation: The values are copied to the caller, then the local r is destroyed.

quiz.prompt: Which is another way to get several values out of a function?
quiz.explanation: The function can write its answers into reference parameters.

quiz.prompt: Why is Student* make() { Student s = {"A", 1}; return &s; } wrong?
options: s is destroyed when the function ends, so the pointer is invalid
quiz.answer: s is destroyed when the function ends, so the pointer is invalid
quiz.explanation: A local variable dies at the end of the function, leaving a dangling pointer.
